title: Combination Sum
description:
Given an array of **distinct** positive integers `candidates` and a positive integer `target`, list every combination of candidates whose values add up to `target`.

A candidate may be used **any number of times**. Two combinations are considered the same if they use the same multiset of values, regardless of order, so each distinct multiset must appear exactly once. Return the combinations in any order.

examples.explanation: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 and 7 = 7. Nothing else works: 6 leaves 1, which no candidate covers.

constraints: The number of valid combinations is below 150.
hints: Think of it as choosing how many copies of each candidate to take, in a fixed candidate order, so a multiset is never produced twice.
Recurse with a `start` index and a `remaining` amount. Pick candidate i >= start, subtract it, and recurse with the *same* start (reuse allowed).
Sort the candidates first; then as soon as candidates[i] > remaining you can `break` out of the loop instead of just `continue`.
signature: def combinationSum(self, candidates: List[int], target: int) -> List[List[int]]:
approach:
**Key insight: generate combinations in non-decreasing candidate order so each multiset has exactly one representation.** Allowing reuse just means the recursive call keeps the same `start` index instead of moving to `i + 1`.

**Algorithm.** Sort `candidates`. `backtrack(start, remaining)`: if `remaining == 0`, record the path. Otherwise loop `i` from `start`; if `candidates[i] > remaining` break (everything after is larger too); else push `candidates[i]`, recurse with `(i, remaining - candidates[i])`, pop.

**Why it works.** Each path is a sorted multiset summing to target, and a sorted multiset corresponds to exactly one sequence of index choices. The `break` is safe only because the array is sorted, which is why sorting is not optional.

**Common mistakes:** recursing with `start + 1` or `0` instead of `i` (the former forbids reuse, the latter produces permutations of the same multiset); using `continue` where `break` would prune the whole rest of the loop; not copying `path` when recording.

**Interview follow-ups:** Only count the combinations instead of listing them? (that is coin-change DP in O(n * target).) Candidates with duplicates and each used once? (Combination Sum II: sort, skip equal neighbours, recurse with `i + 1`.) Can you bound the recursion depth? (at most `target / min(candidates)`.)

complexity.time: O(n^(T/m)) worst case, where T = target and m = smallest candidate
